name: sed
one_line: A stream editor: read lines, change them with rules (mostly search-and-replace), print the result.
plain: A stream editor: read lines, change them with rules (mostly search-and-replace), print the result.
The sections below show when to use it, real examples, and the options explained in plain English.
when: Clean up or transform text in a pipeline: strip prefixes, replace separators, mask secrets.
Print a range of lines from a big file.
Edit a file in place (with a backup).

examples.title: Replace a separator
examples.output:
root | x | 0 | 0 | root | /root | /bin/bash
alice | x | 1001 | 1001 | Alice Lee | /home/alice | /bin/bash

Meeting at 3pm

examples.title: Edit a file in place, with a backup
examples.cmd: cp users.txt copy.txt; sed -i.bak 's/bash/zsh/' copy.txt; diff copy.txt.bak copy.txt
examples.output:
1,2c1,2
< root:x:0:0:root:/root:/bin/bash
< alice:x:1001:1001:Alice Lee:/home/alice:/bin/bash
---
> root:x:0:0:root:/root:/bin/zsh
> alice:x:1001:1001:Alice Lee:/home/alice:/bin/zsh

options.plain: Flags on `s`: all matches / ignore case
Edit the file in place (`-i.bak` keeps a backup)
options.use: Change a file; use a backup suffix

options.plain: Delete / print lines N to M

mistakes: On macOS `sed -i` needs an argument (`sed -i ''`): scripts differ between GNU and BSD sed.
Use a different delimiter for paths: `s#/usr/bin#/opt#`.
`&` in the replacement means the whole match; escape it (`\&`) for a literal ampersand.
sed works line by line; to edit across lines use `-z` or switch to Python.
